newsitem.title: ITALY: O'Dell buried in city which tried to save him.
newsitem.headline: O'Dell buried in city which tried to save him.

text.p: The body of convicted rapist and murderer Joseph O'Dell was buried on Thursday in Palermo, the city which led a vocal but ultimately futile campaign to save him from execution in the United States.
While hundreds turned out for the ceremony, others remained puzzled by Italy's fascination with O'Dell's case and one senator branded the burial a "farce."
O'Dell, who was killed by lethal injection in the state of Virginia last week, was entombed in Palermo's Santa Maria di Gesu cemetery after an emotional Catholic church service.

Around 400 mourners, most of them ordinary Sicilians and many of them young children, crammed into the tiny stuccoed chapel to hear the service, which was also broadcast to more than 100 people sheltering under the shade of pine trees in the picturesque courtyard outside.
O'Dell's widow Lori Urs was there, along with his spiritual advisor Sister Helen Prejean and Palermo's mayor Leoluca Orlando, who flew to the U.S. last week in an 11th hour bid to save O'Dell.

Urs and Prejean, who looked at ease throughout the service, fanned themselves in the stifling heat as they listened to priest Pierto Sorci read a tribute to O'Dell, a man despised by many in his native country as a callous murderer.
"Joseph, brother, welcome to this land of sun, welcome to this city of Palermo, this city of so many problems...," began Sorci, dressed in a priest's purple garb.

"We do not know if you were innocent of the crimes for which you were convicted...We are not even interested...It is not for us to say if you were guilty, and we do not want to make a hero out of you.
"Joseph, you were a sinner, just like those who killed you, who appealed to a law which was written by other sinners.
"Thank-you for choosing this city as your place of rest," Sorci said.

O'Dell's coffin, topped by a single pink lilly, was then carried down the chapel steps to the courtyard outside, where onlookers clapped in tribute to a man who became the focal point for Italy's opposition to the death penalty.

The coffin was lowered into the grave, and only then did Urs weep openly, clutching a silver crucifix on her necklace and kneeling to touch the coffin lid before the stone gravestone was laid in place, sealing O'Dell's corpse in the Sicilian earth.
"Joseph O'Dell III" read the tombstone. "Honorary Citizen of Palermo, Killed by Virginia, U.S.A. in the name of a merciless and brutal justice system. September 20 1941 - July 23 1997."
Urs said afterwards: "I want to be laid to rest in this same chapel. Joseph wanted to be buried in Palermo so as to become a symbol for the fight against the death penalty."
Palermo, more than perhaps any other city in the world, championed the cause of O'Dell, who was executed for the 1985 rape and murder of Helen Schartner.
The city made him an honorary citizen and O'Dell responded by asking for his body to be buried here.
But not everyone was happy with the decision to honour a man who had a long criminal record and no known ties with Italy.
"It's a grotesque farce," senator Valentino Martelli of the rightist National Alliance party said on Wednesday.

"(Prime Minister Romano) Prodi should intervene to stop the world's television from recording this macabre farce in a city which has suddenly forgotten the outrage of children dissolved in acid baths," he said, referring to Palermo's own murky reputation for brutal Mafia murders.
